transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-14
Time: 08:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Evan Park (Redwood AE), Sofia Ramirez (Redwood SE), Amit Rao (Vertex CTO), Janelle Ortiz (ML Eng), Marcus Lee (DevOps)

Summary: quick scoping session to pin the POC sizing: reserved GPUs, burst strategy, and fallback policies. Nolan to run benchma - sorry, Amit will provide sample payloads. Redwood will propose pricing and guardrails.

00:00 Evan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intros - i'm Evan, AE on the account, and with me is Sofia, our solutions engineer.
00:12 Sofia Ramirez: hi all, yeah, good to be here. we'll try to map your workload to a POC that's realistic - reserved baseline + burst.
00:22 Amit Rao: thanks. we want to validate latency and cost for our realtime summarization service. current infra is a mix of hosted endpoints and some on-prem batching for heavy jobs.
00:38 Janelle Ortiz: current traffic is spiky - we see short periods of thousands of requests per minute for live streams, but more commonly it's a steady few hundred.
00:48 Marcus Lee: and for security: we need VPC peering, SSO, and audit logs. SOC2 is a requirement for us.
00:56 Evan Park: got it - SOC2 and VPC noted. for the POC we usually do a 2-week reserved capacity with a small reserved GPU pool to match baseline qps, and configure burst to scale up when needed.
01:10 Sofia Ramirez: to add, our burst uses a separate pool of on-demand GPUs and a routing policy; when reserved queue backs up beyond threshold, we spill to burst capacity. plus we can route to a cheaper quantized model variant as a fallback for best-effort traffic.
01:26 Amit Rao: ok, what's typical reserved size? we want predictable cost but also not to underprovision.
01:34 Sofia Ramirez: usually we ask for your baseline 95th percentile qps and p99 latency target. e g if baseline is 200 qps and you need p99 < 300ms, we'd size reserved to handle the steady 200 with KV cache and batching tuned. then burst covers peak headroom.
01:50 Janelle Ortiz: our baseline is roughly 250 qps, peaks up to 1800 qps for 30-90s windows. p99 target is 350ms end-to-end for the live path.
02:03 Evan Park: okay that's helpful. initial recommendation - reserved pool to cover 250 qps; that maps roughly to 2 x A100-40 or 4 x A10-like GPUs depending on token length and model flavor. for the POC we can propose a conservative 2-reserved-GPU baseline and configure burst to add up to 6 GPUs for short periods.
02:25 Marcus Lee: those numbers seem fine, but curious about cost deltas if we burst that much. how do we cap spend?
02:33 Sofia Ramirez: we include burst policies with hard caps and rate-limits - e g max concurrent burst GPUs and a daily spend cap. also we can set fallbacks so if burst capacity is exhausted we route to a quantized 8-bit model variant or a cheaper region.
02:50 Amit Rao: what's the difference in latency when routing to a quantized variant?
02:55 Sofia Ramirez: depends. quantized 8-bit model often adds 10-30ms at runtime but quality may regress slightly on edge cases. for many summarization prompts it's within acceptable tolerances. we'll include a quality gate in the POC to check for regressions.
03:10 Janelle Ortiz: how do we validate quality and avoid silent regressions?
03:14 Evan Park: we recommend a small eval set from you - maybe 150-300 prompts - and run A/B during the POC. Redwood Optimize can track metric regressions and alert if the quantized variant underperforms beyond a threshold.
03:29 Marcus Lee: network wise, we need to ensure VPC peering and IP allowlists. latency from our region to Redwood region is important.
03:36 Sofia Ramirez: we'll share our VPC network checklist and steps for peering. for the POC we can do a short latency probe as part of the benchmark run to measure RTT and cold-starts.
03:48 Amit Rao: benchmark run - what exactly do you need from us?
03:51 Sofia Ramirez: sample payloads, a representative traffic profile (qps over time), SLO thresholds, and a list of failure modes you care about. we'll run two benchmark types: steady-state throughput and spike/soak tests.
04:05 Evan Park: timeline wise: we'll send a POC proposal Monday with reserved SKU options and burst settings. if you accept, week 1 we stand up reserved capacity and validate connectivity; mid-week run benchmarks; week 2 iterate on tuning and then review results.
04:19 Janelle Ortiz: works for us. one question - how does automatic scaling interact with our internal autoscaler? we use k8s for other services.
04:27 Sofia Ramirez: Redwood's autoscaler is at the model-serving infra layer - it doesn't manage your k8s deployments. for private deployments we can integrate with your autoscaler, but for hosted/dedicated Redwood manages GPU pools and scales models in and out based on queue and latency policies. we expose metrics so you can feed them into your dashboards.
04:46 Marcus Lee: and anything about cold starts when scaling from zero? those temporary latency spikes could break live traffic.
04:52 Sofia Ramirez: we avoid scaling from zero in POC reserved pools; reserved baseline is always warm. for burst we keep a small warm reserve or use quick-start instances to reduce cold-starts. there's also pre-warming hooks if you have predictable windows.
05:08 Amit Rao: acceptable. about fallback policies - can we define high-priority vs low-priority traffic?
05:13 Evan Park: yes - route priority tags. high-priority requests always go to reserved or full-precision variants; low-priority can go to quantized or be rate-limited. we can present a routing matrix in the SOW.
05:27 Janelle Ortiz: what about KV cache sizing? our prompts reuse prefixes a lot because many users share session context.
05:33 Sofia Ramirez: KV cache memory is per-GPU; we'll estimate size based on average sequence length and reuse rate. caching can dramatically reduce compute for repeated prefixes - often a 2-3x cost improvement. we'll ask for sample session lengths to calculate exact numbers.
05:51 Amit Rao: good. security follow-ups - can you share SOC2 and data retention details?
05:55 Evan Park: yep, we'll attach our SOC2 report and data retention policy. for Private deployment we can hand off KMS/HSM integration notes.
06:03 Marcus Lee: what if burst capacity in our region is exhausted - do you fail open or degrade?
06:08 Sofia Ramirez: we implement multi-tier fallback: 1) fall back to quantized model in same region, 2) route to a compatible model in another region (if allowed by data residency), 3) apply rate limits or queue with a graceful 503 with retry-after. we document expected behavior in SLOs.
06:24 Amit Rao: sounds reasonable. benchmarks - can we run a p95/p99 breakdown and token cost numbers?
06:29 Sofia Ramirez: yes, benchmark outputs include p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, tokens/sec, and estimated token cost per 1M tokens. we'll also output regression plots vs your golden prompts.
06:40 Evan Park: i'll include cost models for reserved baseline vs on-demand burst so you can see unit economics.
06:47 Janelle Ortiz: do you support canary rollouts or A/B within the POC?
06:50 Sofia Ramirez: yes, we can do simple A/B routing to compare variants; canary deploys are supported for model version rollouts.
06:59 Amit Rao: ok next steps, to recap - we provide the sample payloads + traffic profile by 2026-02-18; Redwood sends POC SOW + pricing by 2026-02-16; schedule benchmark run on 2026-02-21 10:00 PT.
07:15 Evan Park: correct. i'll also include the fallback and burst caps in the SOW and a suggested reserved SKU mapping.
07:22 Marcus Lee: one last thing - can you put an explicit daily spend cap and an alerting threshold? we want automatic cutoffs if costs exceed X.
07:29 Sofia Ramirez: absolutely - we'll include spend caps and a hard cap that prevents further bursting and an alert flow to notify your oncall.
07:36 Janelle Ortiz: great. thanks everyone.
07:38 Evan Park: thanks all. we'll follow up with docs and the SOW.
07:42 [meeting ends]
